items.definition: The yearly price of borrowing on the card, with most fees included. It is the number to compare two cards by.
items.example: This card has a 24 % APR, which is about 0.066 % a day.

items.definition: The most the bank will let you borrow on the card at one time. Going over it is usually refused and sometimes charged.
items.example: My credit limit is 2000 $, and I use about 600 $ of it.

items.definition: The period between two statements. Everything bought in one cycle appears on the next statement.
items.example: The billing cycle closes on the 12th, so my groceries appear on the 12th statement.

items.definition: The days between the statement date and the due date, during which you can pay in full without interest.
items.example: If I pay the statement balance inside the grace period, I pay no interest.

items.definition: The smallest monthly sum the card will accept. Paying only this keeps the balance, and the interest, alive.
items.example: The minimum payment is 25 $, so the rest of the balance stays on the card.

items.definition: The charge the bank makes for a late payment, on top of any penalty rate and any loss of your good history.
items.example: The late payment cost me a 35 $ overdue fee and my standard rate went up.

items.definition: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.
items.example: Write USD on the invoice, not the word dollar, so the system reads it.

items.definition: The money the law accepts as the final payment of a debt, so that no one can refuse it as the wrong money.
items.example: The landlord must take legal tender for the rent, even when he prefers a transfer.

items.definition: The smaller part of a currency, such as the cent of a dollar, that people rarely see.
items.example: The price is 12.50 dollars, but the money is made of dollars and cents.

items.definition: The value printed on a note or a coin, such as 20 or 500.
items.example: The shop keeps one drawer for the smallest denomination and one for the notes.

items.definition: The price of one currency expressed in the money of another currency.
items.example: Ask which day the exchange rate belongs to, because the number is only true for that day.

items.definition: The currency of the pair that the rate counts from: one unit of it is the thing you exchange.
items.example: In EUR/USD the euro is the base currency and the dollar is the quote currency.

items.definition: The currency of the pair that the rate is expressed in, so the rate says how many units of it you get.
items.example: The rate is given in the quote currency, so a pair written EUR/USD reads in dollars.

items.definition: An arrangement in which several states use one currency and a single authority issues it for all of them.
items.example: The euro area is a currency union, so one central bank issues the notes for every member country.

items.definition: The use, by a country, of the currency of another country as its own money, with no domestic currency issued.
items.example: The country is dollarized: the shops take dollars and nobody issues local notes.

items.definition: The act of lowering the value that other people attach to a person's work or judgement.
items.example: The devaluation was quiet: every meeting began with a small doubt about her work.

items.definition: A country where most payments are still made in cash rather than by card or by transfer.
items.example: In a cash economy, a market stall may not have a machine at all.

items.definition: The market that trades a currency outside the official channel, at a rate the state does not set.
items.example: When the official rate stops working, the parallel market sets the real price of the dollar.

items.definition: The habit of adding a small sum on top of a bill for the person who served you.
items.example: In this restaurant the service charge is on the bill, so there is no tip to add.

items.definition: The money a person working abroad sends to the family at home.
items.example: He sends a remittance every month, and the rent is paid from it.

items.definition: The percentage change in the general level of prices over a period of time, usually a year.
items.example: The annual inflation rate was 4 %, so prices rose 4 % on average.

items.definition: The standard index of the price of a basket of goods and services bought by households. Its change over time is the headline inflation rate.
items.example: The consumer price index is the number the news report quotes.

items.definition: The year the price index starts from, set to 100. Changing it resets the index without changing any actual prices.
items.example: With last year as the base year, the index now stands at 104.

items.definition: Income measured in the money actually received, with no adjustment for changes in prices.
items.example: My nominal income rose, but not as fast as prices.

items.definition: Income adjusted for inflation, which is the figure that says how much you can actually buy.
items.example: Real income fell two per cent because prices rose faster than my pay.

items.definition: The interest rate minus the inflation rate. It is the return a saver actually keeps in purchasing power.
items.example: A 4 % deposit with 6 % inflation gives a real interest rate of minus 2 %.

items.definition: Total pay for the period before any money is deducted for tax, insurance or other agreed deductions.
items.example: My gross pay is 40 $ a month, before anything is taken off.

items.definition: The amount left after all deductions, and the amount that reaches your bank account.
items.example: The difference between my gross and my net is mostly tax and insurance.

items.definition: Any amount taken off gross pay before payment, whether required by law or agreed with you.
items.example: The canteen charge is a deduction, so it comes out before my net pay.

items.definition: Income tax taken out of your pay in advance by the employer. It is not your final tax bill.
items.example: The tax withheld this month was higher because my bonus was large.

items.definition: The compulsory payment into the social insurance system that covers sickness, maternity, accidents and retirement.
items.example: My social insurance contribution is a percentage of my gross pay.

items.definition: Money you paid for work that the company owes you back. It almost always needs a receipt and a deadline.
items.example: I submitted the taxi receipts as an expense claim on Friday.

items.definition: The amount in the account at the start of the statement period. Every figure that follows is measured from it.
items.example: The opening balance was 500 $, so the first transaction was charged against that.

items.definition: The amount in the account at the end of the statement period, after every transaction in it.
items.example: The closing balance is 420 $, which is 80 $ more than the opening balance.

items.definition: Money leaving the account. On a statement it is usually shown with a minus sign or in a column headed money out.
items.example: The debit for the supermarket is 64 $, so that is the debit column, not the credit column.

items.definition: Money arriving in the account, such as a salary or a refund. On a statement it is usually shown with a plus sign.
items.example: The credit of 1200 $ on the 15th is my salary.

items.definition: A payment a company is authorised to take from your account on a date, without asking you again each time.
items.example: The electricity bill is a direct debit, so it leaves my account on the 10th every month.

items.definition: A fixed amount you authorise to be paid on a schedule, whether or not the underlying bill is the same each month.
items.example: I have a standing order to my landlord for the rent, and a direct debit for the utilities.

items.definition: The money of a country: its notes, its coins, and the rules that govern them.
items.example: The shop takes only the local currency.

items.definition: The job money does when it is used to pay for something instead of trading goods for goods.
items.example: The bus ticket is a medium of exchange: the fare buys the ride.
